title: A history of migration to Britain

atoms.b:
((++The_Partition_of_British_India --A_Journey_to_Britain --A_Peaceful_Independence))
In the summer of 1947, the British Empire in South Asia came to an end with enormous violence. The new states of India and Pakistan were born through a process known as The Partition, which forced roughly fifteen million people to abandon their homes and cross newly drawn borders. Up to one million people lost their lives in the violence that followed. Many survivors migrated to Britain.

((++Caribbean_Workers_arrive_in_Britain --Rebuilding_Britian_after_the_First_World_War --The_British_Internationality_Act))
On 22 June 1948, a troopship called the HMT Empire Windrush sailed into Tilbury Docks near London, carrying more than 800 passengers from Caribbean islands such as Jamaica, Trinidad and Barbados. The British government had recently passed the British Nationality Act, which gave all Commonwealth citizens the right to live and work in Britain. The government actively encouraged Caribbean workers to come and help rebuild a country damaged by the Second World War and to staff the newly founded National Health Service.

((++The_Expulsion_of_Uganda's_South_Asians --Britain's_Policy_on_Accepting_Refugees --South_Asians_Leaving_Uganda_for_a_Better_Life))
In August 1972, Uganda's dictator Idi Amin expelled the country's South Asian minority, giving them just 90 days to leave. More than 27,000 Ugandan Asians were resettled in the UK, making them one of the largest single groups of refugees Britain has ever received.

((++Chinese_Settlement_in_Britain --How_Britain's_Restaurant_Industry_Was_Built --Chinatowns:_The_Heart_of_British_City_Life))
Chinese migration has a longer, quieter history. Sailors settled around Limehouse in London's Docklands from the 19th century onwards. After 1945 and especially after Hong Kong's “New Territories” opened to emigration in the 1950s, thousands of Cantonese-speaking migrants opened restaurants and laundries, laying the foundations of today's Chinatowns in London, Manchester and Liverpool.

The United Kingdom is one of the most ethnically ((++diverse --homogenous)) countries in Europe, and the 2021 Census revealed just how quickly that diversity is ((++growing --shrinking)). According to the Office for National Statistics, 81.7% of people in England and Wales identified as ((++White --Asian)) in 2021, compared to 86.0% a decade earlier. The remaining 18% described themselves as Black, Asian, Mixed or Other — up from 13.8% in 2011.

The ((++largest --smallest)) minority group is now Asian, Asian British or Asian Welsh, which rose from 7.5% (4.2 million) in 2011 to 9.3% (5.5 million) in 2021. People ((++identifying_as --married_to)) Black, Black British, Caribbean or African made up 4.2% of the English population, while Mixed or Multiple ethnic groups accounted for 3.0%.
